lessons.title: A Practical Framework for Choosing Between Equity and Debt

children.text: Four chapters of mechanics come down to one decision that a founder, a CFO or a treasury team has to actually take: this requirement, this quarter, funded how? The honest answer is rarely "equity is better" or "debt is cheaper". It depends on eight things, and they can be worked through in an afternoon.
This lesson gives you that framework, and the arithmetic to go with it.

body.text: Do not start by asking which is cheaper. Start by asking what the money is for, how certain its returns are, and what happens to the company if the next two years go badly. The funding choice follows from those answers.

children.text: The Eight Tests

cells: 1. Certainty of returns
The cash flows from this spending are contracted or highly predictable
The outcome is genuinely uncertain, or years away
2. Timing
The money comes back within a defined period you can match a tenure to
The payback is open-ended or the business may pivot
3. Bad-year servicing
The business can pay interest and principal from its worst recent year's cash flow
A bad year would make fixed payments impossible
4. Security
There are assets, receivables or guarantees a lender will accept
The business is asset-light with nothing to charge
5. Return versus cost
Return on capital employed comfortably exceeds the after-tax cost of debt
Returns are below or close to the cost of debt
6. Ownership appetite
Owners want to keep control and future upside
Owners will trade ownership for capability, network or risk sharing
7. Existing leverage
Debt to EBITDA is below industry norms with headroom left
The company is already at or beyond its comfortable limit
8. Speed and certainty
A sanctioned limit or an existing lender can move quickly
The raise is large enough that a full process is worth the months

body.text: Tests 1, 2 and 3 are about the business. Tests 4 to 8 are about the company's current position. If the first three point to equity, the rest do not matter much: no amount of collateral makes fixed repayments safe for a business with unpredictable cash flows.

children.text: The Number Most Companies Never Calculate
Lenders will tell you what they are willing to sanction. That is not the same as what you can safely carry. A company's
debt capacity
starts from sustainable earnings, not from the sanction letter.

markDefs.definition: The most a business can borrow while still servicing it comfortably in a bad year, not the most a lender is willing to sanction.

body.caption: Sustainable means a normal year, not the best one

children.text: Take a company with sustainable EBITDA of ₹30 crore that has decided, looking at its industry peers and the stability of its revenue, that it does not want debt above 2.5 times EBITDA. It already carries ₹40 crore of debt.

body.title: Find the headroom
body.prompt: Sustainable EBITDA is ₹30 crore, the target ceiling is 2.5 times EBITDA, and existing debt is ₹40 crore. How much more can this company borrow within its own limit, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: Total capacity is ₹30 crore times 2.5, which is ₹75 crore. Less the ₹40 crore already borrowed, the headroom is ₹35 crore. Anything beyond that should be funded with equity or internal accruals, whatever a bank may be willing to sanction.

children.text: Then stress it. Capacity calculated on a normal year means nothing if the business cannot service that debt in a bad one.

body.title: Stress the capacity
body.prompt: At full capacity of ₹75 crore borrowed at 10%, interest is ₹7.5 crore a year. In its worst recent year the company generated EBITDA of ₹18 crore. What is interest cover in that bad year? Answer to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹18 crore divided by ₹7.5 crore is 2.4 times. Against a typical covenant floor of 2x, that survives a repeat of the worst year, which is exactly the test to apply before borrowing to the limit. Had the worst year produced ₹12 crore of EBITDA, cover would be 1.6x and the capacity number would need to come down.

body.text: Notice that this calculation never asked what the bank was willing to lend. Companies that borrow to the sanctioned limit rather than to their own capacity are the ones renegotiating covenants two years later.

children.text: The Order Most Companies Should Follow
Before choosing between equity and debt, check whether the requirement can be met without either.
Internal accruals.
Free, instant, and nobody's permission needed.
Working capital discipline.
Faster collections, leaner inventory and better supplier terms often release more cash than the loan being contemplated.
Existing sanctioned limits.
Undrawn headroom is cheaper and faster than a new facility.
Fresh debt.
Term loans matched to asset life, or working capital facilities matched to the cash cycle.
Hybrids.
When valuation cannot be agreed yet, or the investor needs downside protection.
New equity.
When the risk genuinely should be shared, or when debt capacity is exhausted.
This sequence is the practical version of the
pecking order

from Chapter 1. It is not a rule of nature, and there are good reasons to break it, especially for a loss-making business that cannot borrow at all. But a company that reaches for an equity round before tightening its receivables is usually solving the wrong problem at the highest possible price.

markDefs.definition: The observed tendency of companies to fund themselves first from internal cash, then debt, and only last from new equity.

children.text: Four Mistakes That Recur

body.title: The common error, and what to do instead

columns.label: What goes wrong
points: Funding a ten-year asset with three-year money
Borrowing against a forecast rather than a track record
Selling equity to cover a temporary working capital gap
Optimising for the headline valuation rather than the terms

columns.label: What good practice looks like
points: Match tenure to asset life, so the asset pays for its own funding
Size debt to your worst recent year, and equity to the uncertain upside
Fix the cash cycle first, then use a working capital facility
Model the fully diluted cap table and the covenant headroom before signing

body.label: What an asset-liability mismatch cost India
body.context: Several Indian non-bank lenders had funded long-dated infrastructure and property loans with short-term commercial paper, refinancing every few months. When confidence broke after the IL&FS default in September 2018, that short-term money stopped being available and the mismatch became a liquidity crisis across the sector. The underlying assets had not suddenly become worthless. The funding structure simply could not survive a pause in refinancing.

children.text: An
asset-liability mismatch
is a funding decision, not a market event. It is created at sanction, and it is discovered years later at the worst possible moment.

markDefs.definition: Funding long-life assets with short-term borrowing, so the company depends on repeatedly refinancing before the asset has produced its returns.

body.title: Apply the framework
body.question: A profitable Ludhiana garment exporter wants ₹6 crore to fund a confirmed 5-month order from a long-standing European buyer. It has stock, receivables and two years of headroom on its debt to EBITDA. What does the framework say?
options: Equity, because export orders are risky
Debt, specifically a short-term working capital facility or invoice discounting matched to the order cycle
Nothing, the order should be declined
body.explanation: Tests 1, 2 and 3 all point to debt: the cash flow is contracted, the timing is defined at five months, and the business is profitable with headroom. Security exists in the stock and receivables. Selling equity permanently to fund a five-month cash gap would be the most expensive possible answer.

body.title: The harder case
body.question: A profitable ₹90 crore revenue specialty chemicals company wants ₹50 crore to enter an unrelated product category where it has no experience, no customers and expects losses for three years. It has collateral and its bank has indicated it would lend. What is the right analysis?
options: Borrow, because the bank is willing and debt is cheaper
The availability of debt is not the test. Uncertain, loss-making, multi-year outcomes should be funded with equity or internal accruals, not fixed repayments
body.explanation: A lender being willing is test 4, not tests 1 to 3. Three years of expected losses means interest would be serviced by the existing business, putting a working company at risk for an unproven one. Fund it with equity, with internal accruals, or in smaller stages that prove the category before committing ₹50 crore.

body.title: Match the money
body.textWithBlank: The tenure of any borrowing should be matched to the ___ of the asset or need it is funding.
body.explanation: Short needs get short money and long assets get long money. Breaking this creates an asset-liability mismatch, which is survivable until refinancing becomes difficult, at which point it is not.

body.title: A one-page scoring method, if you want something mechanical

children.text: For a requirement you are actually evaluating, score each of the eight tests from minus 2 to plus 2, where plus 2 strongly favours debt and minus 2 strongly favours equity. Weight tests 1, 2 and 3 double, because they concern the business itself rather than its current position.
A strongly positive total points to debt, most likely matched to the asset or cash cycle.
A strongly negative total points to equity, or to not doing the project yet.
A total near zero usually means the requirement should be split: part debt for the secured, predictable portion, and part equity or internal accruals for the uncertain portion.

The scoring is a discussion tool, not an oracle. Its real value is forcing a board to say out loud which test it is relying on, because most bad funding decisions come from a single test being quietly ignored.

body.title: Three requirements, one board meeting
body.scenario: You are the finance head of a profitable Nashik food processing company. Revenue is ₹260 crore, sustainable EBITDA ₹32 crore, existing debt ₹45 crore at 9.5%, net worth ₹140 crore, and the worst EBITDA in the past seven years was ₹19 crore. The board is considering three proposals in the same meeting. A: ₹40 crore for a new cold chain facility with contracted offtake from two large retail chains, asset life about twelve years, expected return around 15%. B: ₹25 crore to launch a direct-to-consumer brand with no existing customer base, expected losses for two to three years. C: ₹15 crore of additional working capital because a large customer has moved to 90-day terms.
body.prompt: Take each proposal through the framework and recommend a funding plan for the meeting.
body.modelAnswer:
First, the company-level number. At a target of 2.5 times EBITDA, capacity is ₹80 crore, so headroom over the existing ₹45 crore is ₹35 crore. All three proposals together need ₹80 crore, which is well beyond that. The board cannot fund everything with debt, so the framework must also rank.

Proposal A, cold chain: contracted offtake, defined asset life, 15% return against an after-tax cost of debt of roughly 7%. Tests 1 to 5 all point to debt. Fund with a term loan of about ₹40 crore over ten to twelve years, secured on the facility itself. Check cover at the worst year: interest on ₹85 crore of total debt at around 10% is ₹8.5 crore, against a worst-year EBITDA of ₹19 crore, which is about 2.2x. Tight but survivable, and the new facility adds EBITDA of its own from year one. Consider funding ₹5 to ₹10 crore from internal accruals to keep the ratio comfortable.

Proposal B, the D2C brand: no customers, two to three years of losses, no security, and the return is unknown rather than merely uncertain. Every one of the first three tests points away from debt. Options: fund it from internal accruals in stages tied to milestones, bring in an equity investor for that business specifically, or defer it. My recommendation would be to start with a much smaller committed amount, perhaps ₹3 to ₹5 crore from accruals, prove the unit economics, and only then decide whether it deserves ₹25 crore of anyone's money.

Proposal C, working capital: this is not a growth decision, it is a cash cycle problem created by a customer. Before borrowing, test whether the receivable can be discounted on TReDS at the customer's credit rather than the company's, which would be cheaper and would not consume debt capacity. If a facility is still needed, take a working capital limit sized to the cycle, not a term loan.

Recommendation to the board: approve A with debt, meet C through receivable financing first and a limit only if needed, and stage B out of internal accruals. That keeps total leverage near the company's own ceiling instead of a lender's, and it puts fixed repayments only against contracted cash flows.

body.title: The funding decision scorecard
steps: What exactly is the money for, and when does it come back?
How certain are those returns: contracted, likely, or hopeful?
Can we service this in our worst year of the past five to seven years?
What is our debt capacity, calculated from sustainable EBITDA rather than from a sanction letter?
Does the return on this spending exceed our after-tax cost of debt?
Does the tenure on offer match the life of what we are funding?
Have we exhausted internal accruals, working capital discipline and undrawn limits first?
What does the cap table or the covenant position look like after this, and after the next raise?

body.label: MCA: View Company or LLP Master Data
body.description: Look up any Indian company's registered charges to see what is already pledged and to which lender. Useful before assuming an asset is available as security, and useful for understanding how much a potential partner or customer has already borrowed.

cards.definition: Sustainable EBITDA times a target debt-to-EBITDA multiple, less existing debt.
A normal year's operating profit, not the best year, used as the base for capacity.
Can interest and principal be paid from the worst recent year's cash flow?
Funding an asset with borrowing whose repayment period matches the asset's life.
Funding long assets with short money, creating dependence on refinancing.
Internal accruals first, then debt, then new equity.
Borrow only while return on capital employed exceeds the after-tax cost of debt.
The gap between current debt and the level at which the company stops being comfortable.

points: Start with what the money is for and how certain its returns are, not with which source looks cheaper.
Three business tests dominate: certainty of returns, timing, and whether a bad year can still service the debt.
Calculate debt capacity from sustainable EBITDA, then stress it against your worst recent year.
What a lender will sanction is not a measure of what a company can safely carry.
Work down the order: internal accruals, working capital discipline, undrawn limits, new debt, hybrids, then equity.
Match tenure to asset life. Mismatches are created quietly at sanction and discovered in a refinancing squeeze.
Split requirements where the answer is mixed: debt for the contracted part, equity or accruals for the uncertain part.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, legal or tax advice. The framework is a structured way to think, not a substitute for company-specific analysis. Target leverage multiples, covenant floors and cost assumptions vary widely by industry and lender. All companies used are fictional illustrations.
